items.title: 11.1 Domains and Ranges of Sine and Cosine Functions

blocks.text: In this unit we explore key ideas that show the role of trigonometry in mathematics and in real life. We begin by learning how to find the domain and range of the trigonometric functions, which tells us how they behave. Next we discuss even and odd functions and their periodicity, which explains their repeating patterns.

Then we learn to draw and analyse the graphs of the sine, cosine and tangent functions. After this we calculate the maximum and minimum values of sinusoidal functions and study their special properties such as amplitude, frequency and phase shift.

Finally, these ideas are applied to practical problems in navigation, engineering and physics, such as calculating distances, choosing the best angle for a solar panel and analysing forces in structures. Let us first find the domains and ranges of the trigonometric functions before drawing their graphs.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two words are used throughout this unit:
Domain: the set of all inputs that a function accepts (the values of \(\theta\) for which the function has a value).
Range: the set of all outputs that the function actually gives.
Think of a function as a machine. The domain is everything you may put in; the range is everything that can come out. For example, for \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\) (real values only) the domain is \(x \ge 0\) and the range is \(y \ge 0\).

We have already defined the trigonometric functions \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\), \(\tan\theta\), \(\csc\theta\), \(\sec\theta\) and \(\cot\theta\). We know that if \(P(x, y)\) is any point on the unit circle with centre at the origin \(O\) such that \(m\angle XOP = \theta\) is in standard position, then

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Unit circle means a circle of radius 1. In the right triangle \(OMP\) the hypotenuse is \(OP = 1\), so
\[\cos\theta = \dfrac{OM}{OP} = \dfrac{x}{1} = x\]
\[\sin\theta = \dfrac{MP}{OP} = \dfrac{y}{1} = y\]
This is why the unit circle is so useful: the coordinates of \(P\) are exactly \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\), and the signs of \(x\) and \(y\) automatically give the signs in every quadrant.

\(\Rightarrow\) for any real number \(\theta\) there is one and only one value of each \(x\) and \(y\), i.e., of each \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\).
Hence \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) are the functions of \(\theta\) and their domain is \(\mathbb{R}\), the set of real numbers.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is every real number allowed? Here \(\theta\) is measured in radians, so it is a real number. Whatever \(\theta\) is (positive, negative, bigger than \(2\pi\), a fraction), we can rotate the terminal side \(OP\) through that angle, and it always cuts the unit circle at exactly one point \(P\). That point has one \(x\) and one \(y\), so \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) always exist and are unique.
Nothing is ever divided in \(x\) or \(y\), so there is no value of \(\theta\) to exclude.

Since \(P(x, y)\) is a point on the unit circle with centre at the origin \(O\), therefore
\[-1 \le x \le 1 \quad \text{and} \quad -1 \le y \le 1\]
\[\Rightarrow -1 \le \cos\theta \le 1\]
\[\text{and} \quad -1 \le \sin\theta \le 1\]
Thus, the range of sine and cosine functions is \([-1, 1]\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why can \(x\) and \(y\) not go beyond \(-1\) and \(1\)? Every point of the unit circle satisfies \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 1\). Since \(y^{2} \ge 0\), we get \(x^{2} \le 1\), so \(-1 \le x \le 1\). In the same way \(-1 \le y \le 1\).
Also, every number between \(-1\) and \(1\) is actually reached: as \(P\) goes once round the circle, \(x\) moves continuously from \(1\) down to \(-1\) and back, and so does \(y\). So the range is the whole closed interval \([-1, 1]\), end points included.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
Use the range to spot impossible equations at once. \(\sin\theta = 2\) or \(\cos\theta = -1.5\) has no solution, because the value lies outside \([-1, 1]\).
But \(\sin\theta = 1\) and \(\cos\theta = -1\) are possible (at \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\theta = \pi\)): the end points belong to the range.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. On the unit circle, \(\cos\theta = x\) and \(\sin\theta = y\), where \(P(x, y)\) is on the terminal side of \(\theta\).
2. Domain of \(\sin\) and \(\cos\): \(\mathbb{R}\), all real numbers.
3. Range of \(\sin\) and \(\cos\): \([-1, 1]\), i.e. \(-1 \le \sin\theta \le 1\) and \(-1 \le \cos\theta \le 1\).
4. The extreme values: \(\sin\theta = 1\) at \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), \(-1\) at \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\); \(\cos\theta = 1\) at \(0\), \(-1\) at \(\pi\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Mixing up domain and range: the domain is about \(\theta\) (input), the range is about \(\sin\theta\) or \(\cos\theta\) (output).
2. Writing the range as \((-1, 1)\) with round brackets. The values \(-1\) and \(1\) are reached, so square brackets \([-1, 1]\) are needed.
3. Thinking that \(\theta\) itself must lie between \(0\) and \(2\pi\). Any real angle is allowed; only the output is limited.
